entry.title: How OpenAI's Performance Factory Keeps ChatGPT Fast (15 minute read)
entry.content:
When ChatGPT slows down, one Codex session investigates and a second tries to rule out its explanation before a fix is proposed. In one case, the reviewer reopened an investigation after noticing that the service blamed for failed image downloads had already recovered while the downloads were still failing. Engineers decide what ships, and Codex checks whether performance returns to baseline after deployment.

entry.title: Stripe Evals for Real-World Coding Agent Performance (13 minute read)
entry.content:
Stripe tested coding agents on one-time payments, subscriptions, and Connect integrations. Agents met 78.1% of required criteria on average, but only 29.4% of runs met every required criterion. All 14 agent setups scored higher with Stripe's plugin.

From TLDR Dev · 2026-11-20 · Articles & Tutorials

entry.title: Distributed, High-Performance Blob Storage on SQLite (12 minute read)
entry.content:
Zerodha built Blobasaur, a Redis-compatible store that shards compressed UI preferences across SQLite files and batches writes per shard. In a memory-backed benchmark with 64 KiB JSON payloads, moving from one shard to 16 raised write throughput from about 7,700 to 25,300 operations per second. Cluster slots are configured statically, with offline resharding and no automatic failover.

entry.title: Top 10 Things AI Gets Wrong in Web Development (10 minute read)
entry.content:
Coding agents passed 52% of Chrome's web development checks on their own and 91% with Modern Web Guidance installed. Common misses included restoring keyboard focus when a dialog closes, respecting reduced-motion preferences during smooth scrolling, and reserving space for content that loads later.

entry.title: When Can You Ship on Offline Evals Alone? (10 minute read)
entry.content:
Spotify explores when offline AI evaluations can support a launch decision without an A/B test. In its working example, measurement noise makes the offline eval appear to explain 24% of the variance in online effects when the modeled value is 60%. The proposed rule sends borderline changes to A/B tests and randomly audits some other decisions to detect drift.

entry.title: PostgreSQL 19 Released (6 minute read)
entry.content:
PostgreSQL 19 introduces concurrent table repacking to reclaim space while reads and writes continue. It also lets applications wait for a standby to replay a specific write and return an existing row directly when an insert conflicts, simplifying get-or-create queries.

entry.content:

In synthetic tests with background chatter and bursts of noise, the old pipeline waited 6 to 10 seconds after the last word, while the new one waited 1 to 1.6 seconds.

entry.title: Why Chrome Still Uses the Old IP After You Edit Your Hosts File (4 minute read)
entry.content:
Chrome can reuse a connection to the old IP after a hosts file edit because it pools connections by hostname and port. A used socket can stay open for five idle minutes, and flushing Chrome's socket pools forces a fresh lookup but also closes unrelated connections in the same profile.

entry.content:

With the same repository instructions and tools, Gemini queried a code graph while Claude generally searched from the shell, illustrating why teams should retest behavior after a model swap.

entry.title: The Magic of Partial Evaluation (12 minute read)
entry.content:
Partial evaluation executes the parts of a program whose inputs are already known and leaves specialized code for the remaining work. This post has examples that build from arithmetic and schema validation to the Futamura projections, showing how specializing an interpreter can produce compiled programs and even a compiler.

entry.content:
CSS random() can give elements distinct values that stay consistent across breakpoints and animations. This worked example explains how cache keys, property positions, and explicit scopes determine whether random values are shared, regenerated, or fixed for debugging.

entry.title: Sashiko: Lessons from Building an Agentic Code Review System for Linux (10 minute read)
entry.content:
Sashiko separates specialist bug discovery from verification, requiring code evidence for both findings and dismissals. Its review pipeline gathers surrounding context, investigates uncertain cases individually, and publishes its reasoning, with production data showing a correlation between clean reviews and fewer follow-up fixes.

entry.title: We Stopped a Railway Migration Three Weeks Out (10 minute read)
entry.content:
A production migration was canceled after database import times and operational constraints made the cutover too difficult to predict. The retrospective argues for pricing recovery, observability, storage limits, and maintenance work alongside compute, while noting that its import runs were not a controlled within-tier benchmark.

entry.title: The Codebase Is the Harness (2 minute read)
entry.content:
Agent tooling, instructions, review processes, and product code can evolve together inside one repository. One workflow uses session recordings to diagnose user-facing bugs and then updates instructions after fixes, with a person still setting the broader direction.

entry.title: Traffic Mix Matters (2 minute read)
entry.content:
A load test can miss production failures when it reproduces request volume without reproducing workload distribution. Interactive simulations show key concentration reducing throughput in a lock-based system but improving it in a cached system, so the same skew can move performance in opposite directions.

entry.title: Why Is Gemini 4 Carbon Taking So Long? (5 minute read)
entry.content:
Traces from a private bug-fixing evaluation attribute Carbon's long runtimes to slower inference, unnecessary investigation, and repeated file reads. About half its steps addressed work outside the tickets, while periodic check-ins shortened one trial from 37 to 28 minutes, suggesting that stopping behavior contributes to the gap.

entry.title: Advancing Chip Design with OpenAI Models (5 minute read)
entry.content:
OpenAI reports model-written RTL improvements across its Jalapeño chip and AMD designs, including up to 14% improvement in power, performance, and area relative to heavily optimized GPU baselines. Separate RISC-V evaluations found stronger results when models were designed from specifications, though omitted features and simplified timing checks limit how directly those scores transfer to production.

When static analysis stalls, it shifts to one recorded hypothesis at a time, using probes or logs to prove or disprove explanations instead of letting the agent keep guessing.

entry.title: Should You Actually Add AI to That? (15 minute read)
entry.content:
An AI feature should return more value through reduced effort, fewer errors, or greater consistency than users spend adapting to and verifying it. A four-question audit checks total effort, performance against the existing method, whether users can catch errors, and whether they retain that judgment after prolonged use.

From TLDR Dev · 2026-11-18 · Articles & Tutorials

entry.title: How the Claude Code Team Thinks About Verification (9 minute read)
entry.content:
The Claude Code team treats verification as running the changed system and collecting evidence, with end-to-end, property, and differential tests providing complementary checks. Its workflow keeps review rules outside the change being judged, runs cheap checks before shared CI, and turns recurring failures into rules evaluated against past incidents and stable changes.

From TLDR Dev · 2026-11-18 · Articles & Tutorials

entry.title: Not Everything Needs an LLM (7 minute read)
entry.content:
PostHog uses decision models to gate expensive LLM calls, route requests, and rerank search results with explicit probability scores. Its personal-information checks let 98.7% of session summaries skip a rewriting call, but thresholds need calibration for each task and model because false positives and false negatives carry different costs.

From TLDR Dev · 2026-11-18 · Opinions & Advice

entry.title: How Can You Be Responsible for Code You Don't Understand? (5 minute read)
entry.content:
Teams delegating all coding and review to AI gradually lose the familiarity and skills needed to maintain that code themselves. Treat accountability as responsibility for measurable system outcomes. Reversing an AI mandate will not instantly restore those skills.

entry.content:

entry.title: From Skiplists to B+ Trees: Making Valkey Sorted Sets More Memory Efficient (7 minute read)
entry.content:
Valkey 9.2 replaces large sorted sets' skiplist index with a B+ tree that packs entries together and uses SIMD-assisted searches. In a five-million-member test, per-member index overhead fell by 36% to 43%, while command behavior stayed the same. The release is still in candidate testing.

entry.title: Squircles (6 minute read)
entry.content:
Squircles that look similar can have very different curvature, and Figma's approximation contains discontinuities where its curves join. This article contains an interactive comparison that explains the tradeoffs between Apple, Figma, clothoid, and superellipse shapes, along with the CSS for approximating Apple's corners using corner-shape.

From TLDR Dev · 2026-11-17 · Articles & Tutorials

entry.title: What Does It Mean to Understand What We Built? (2 minute read)
entry.content:
Understanding individual lines of code does not necessarily explain a system's behavior, especially emergent failures. AI could help engineers focus on system properties and develop better tools for understanding what they actually built.

entry.title: From Tasks to Goals (6 minute read)
entry.content:
Giving an agent an ongoing goal means delegating decisions about which tasks to do and when to act. That requires tool boundaries, feedback, persistent memory, and ways to ask questions, plus stopping rules that let the agent do nothing when no action is useful.

From TLDR Dev · 2026-11-17 · Opinions & Advice

entry.title: How Rust Changed Me as a Developer (10 minute read)
entry.content:
Rust's enums make variants explicit and let the compiler enforce that every case is handled. This essay explores how sum types and static dispatch change abstraction choices, including when a straightforward enum is more useful than designing an interface.

From TLDR Dev · 2026-11-17 · Opinions & Advice

entry.title: How to Speed Up CI in the Age of AI-Written Code (8 minute read)
entry.content:
AI coding agents produce code faster than CI pipelines can check it, turning long pipelines into queues for developers and agents. Five fixes target the bottleneck: measure slow steps, cache dependencies, use faster runners, parallelize jobs and tests, and skip redundant work with path filters and cancellation. Change one thing at a time and check vendor speed claims against your own pipeline.

From TLDR Dev · 2026-11-16 · Articles & Tutorials

entry.title: Let's Write a PostScript Interpreter (14 minute read)
entry.content:
Build a small PostScript interpreter in JavaScript, starting with tokenization, operand and dictionary stacks, and representations for names, arrays, and procedures. This tutorial adds execution and an interactive REPL, then explores recursion, iteration, and dynamic scope. It deliberately omits graphics, strings, most error handling, and other parts of the full language.

From TLDR Dev · 2026-11-16 · Articles & Tutorials

entry.title: Goal Engineering: How to Design Goals (5 minute read)
entry.content:
Agent feedback becomes a bottleneck when expert knowledge and subjective preferences live only in people's heads. Scope goals around what humans can review efficiently, rather than simply giving each agent more context. In the Actively AI case study, agents organized by job type across accounts let salespeople review similar tasks together and share lessons across their work.

From TLDR Dev · 2026-11-16 · Articles & Tutorials

entry.title: All AI-generated code should be Open Source (2 minute read)
entry.content:
This essay argues that AI-generated code should be released under open-source licenses or dedicated to the public domain because models depend on collectively produced code. It also raises copyright questions while acknowledging that jurisdictions differ and that human involvement varies. The proposal is an argument about how developers should share generated work.

The examples are constructed rather than a controlled AI experiment, and Markdown guidance still needs maintenance and accessibility review.

entry.content:

Dates indicate roughly when titles became common and are estimates rather than a sourced chronology.

entry.title: How we cut Next.js memory from ~5GB to ~1GB: the react-query timer holding every SSR request (9 minute read)
entry.content:
Zepto's Next.js pods sat at about 5 GB because react-query v3 starts a multi-minute cache timer for every query rendered on the server, and Node ties each timer to the request's AsyncLocalStorage context, keeping every finished request in memory. Building server-side queries with an infinite cache time stopped the timers and dropped pods to about 1.2 GB, and the same trap still applies on v5 when hooks set an explicit gcTime. The fix also exposed that autoscaling had been driven by the leak, so teams fixing memory issues should watch replica counts and latency afterward.
